intro.headline: I make coding agents fail loudly.
paragraphs: I'm YuGiMob. I build extensions for pi, the terminal coding agent, and publish them on npm. This page is where they live, each with a demo you can run.

The pattern behind all of them is the same. An agent changes a file that looks right and is subtly wrong, or runs a command a human would have paused on. Most fixes are better prompts and good intentions. I would rather move the failure into the tool, where it can be refused, caught, or made impossible.

If you run coding agents against real repositories, you have watched at least one of these failures happen. Each tool below starts with the problem it exists to kill; the benchmark at the end was how I checked my own work, including the runs I lose.

problems.name: pi-hashline-edit-pro
problems.headline: The edit lands on the wrong line
problems.problem: Line numbers shift the moment anything above them changes, and fuzzy matching will happily edit a similar block somewhere else. The agent reports success, the diff looks plausible, and the mistake surfaces three edits later.
problems.answer: Every served line gets its own four-letter anchor from a table built for tokenizers, and an edit names anchors instead of line numbers or fuzzy text. The extension registers read, replace, replace_match, insert, copy, move, grep, and undo_last_change; copy and move cross files, same-message edits to one file batch into one atomic change, and a line that changed on disk is refused with [E_RANGE_STALE] and re-served for the retry. Undo is single-level, per file, and survives a restart.
highlights: Anchors survive inserts, deletes, and re-reads
Stale edits are refused, not guessed
replace_match edits inside a line without retyping it
copy and move work across files
Same-message edits batch into one undoable change

problems.name: pi-unsloth-webtools
problems.headline: Web access costs a key and returns soup
problems.problem: Almost every way to give an agent the web wants an API key, a paid tier, or a browser farm. When it finally fetches something, it hands the model a wall of navigation, cookie banners, and tracking scripts, and calls that reading.
problems.answer: Two tools, both keyless: web_search sweeps DuckDuckGo and Startpage by default, canonicalizes the hrefs, and fuses each engine's own ordering, while web_fetch normalizes the URL, extracts HTML or PDF text to Markdown with page metadata, and retries a refusal through a browser-fingerprint transport. A page that only exists after JavaScript runs is rendered locally with Lightpanda; nothing is sent to a third-party renderer. Localhost and local files work by default, and the resolved-IP SSRF guard is an opt-in setting.
highlights: DuckDuckGo and Startpage by default, Yandex opt-in
HTML-to-Markdown, PDF text, and page metadata
Browser-fingerprint transport for refused pages
Lightpanda renders JavaScript pages locally
Local files and private addresses allowed by default

problems.name: pi-tor-proxy
problems.headline: Agent traffic leaks where it comes from
problems.problem: The moment an agent fetches a URL, your IP and your resolver are part of the request. Setting one proxy variable is not a privacy story, and a shared circuit links every request back to the same exit, which is its own kind of fingerprint.
problems.answer: The extension downloads its own Tor binary, verifies it against a SHA-256 hash, and routes every request through it. Each pi instance authenticates with its own SOCKS username, so IsolateSOCKSAuth gives it a separate circuit and exit IP, and the exit is verified against check.torproject.org. /tor-cycle swaps the exit, /tor-country and /tor-exclude constrain which exits are used, and loopback stays out of the proxy so local tooling keeps working. Linux and macOS only.
highlights: Self-managed, hash-verified Tor binary
Per-instance circuit via IsolateSOCKSAuth
Exit IP verified against check.torproject.org
/tor-cycle, /tor-country, and /tor-exclude
Loopback stays out of the proxy

problems.name: pi-msg-workflow
problems.headline: Long runs forget the plan
problems.problem: Ask an agent to review a change in three passes and the original plan, the corrections, and the review comments all dissolve into one context window. By the last round it is negotiating with a summary of a summary, and the thing you asked for first is somewhere in the middle.
problems.answer: Numbered message and command stores keep the plan outside the conversation, and /workflow-edit changes it in place. A workflow is a start phase, one or more review rounds that reset the context between passes, and a final commit or summary; rounds carry optional retries, skip-when-unchanged gates, and an early exit once a review converges. Six workflows ship by default, and each round sees the messages it needs, not the entire history.
highlights: /msg, /cmd, and /workflow
Numbered, editable message and command stores
Rounds reset the context between passes
The /workflow-edit overlay
Six workflows ship by default

problems.name: pi-git-commit
problems.headline: The agent commits like it owns the repo
problems.problem: An agent with shell access will eventually run git commit -am "fix", or stage a file you never looked at. A rule in a prompt is not a guardrail; it is a wish with good manners.
problems.answer: The bash guard blocks mutative git commands before they run. Commits go through a structured git_commit tool with a type (FIX, IMPROVE, NEW) and a message, and the flow only opens after a human runs /commit; /amend rewrites the last commit's message through git_amend, and /stop-commit closes either flow. The gated tools stay listed all session, so the provider prompt cache survives. The agent can prepare the commit; it cannot decide to make it.
highlights: Mutative git commands in bash are blocked
FIX, IMPROVE, and NEW typed commits
The flow opens only after /commit or /amend
The tool set never changes mid-session
One guard instead of prompt heroics

evidence.name: pi-edit-benchmark
evidence.headline: One benchmark I did not write, one I did
evidence.problem: Editing-tool READMEs ship with a demo GIF and a claim, and almost none of them publish the runs where they lose. If the only evidence is a highlight reel, it is not evidence; it is marketing with extra steps.
evidence.answer: pi-edit-benchmark drives real models through each tool's own tools and scores correctness, safety, and robustness. The headline number is a pass rate; the staleness split is scored separately, where a refusal passes and a stale edit that recovers after a re-read still counts, while a silent wrong-line edit is the worst failure class. Every contender links to a committed trace, including the runs my own tool fails.
highlights: Stale scenarios are scored separately
A refusal can pass; a recovery still counts
Every contender links to a committed trace
Confidence intervals on every pass rate
The losses are published too
evidence.intro: Two checks, in order of independence. The first is third-party: alexshpunt's Explicit Edit Benchmark scores the tool without me. The second is mine: pi-edit-benchmark, kept as a dated snapshot with a committed trace for every run, including the ones I lose.

external.note: Maintained by alexshpunt. I did not write the tasks or the scoring rule; the number is the median across the complete model-route configurations.

evidence.disclosure: I wrote pi-edit-benchmark, so read it as a regression suite with receipts, not neutral evidence.

principles: Make the wrong operation impossible, not merely discouraged.
Show the model exactly what it sees.
Put a human gate in front of anything destructive.
Measure before claiming, and publish the traces.
Keep the site static; let a scheduled job refresh the numbers.
colophon: I started building these because I kept watching agents do plausible-looking damage. Not crashes; worse. A rename that missed one call site, a commit nobody reviewed, a fetch that sent my address to a stranger. Each extension closes one of those holes in a way a prompt cannot.

The tools are hand-written TypeScript, published on npm under MIT (the web tools are AGPL). The numbers on this page are pulled from the GitHub and npm APIs every day by a scheduled workflow, so the stars and downloads are measured, not maintained.
No framework, no build step, no runtime dependencies. Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, served straight from GitHub Pages.
